cells.verb: catching fire before it knows what for
cells.place: in the quiet hour where you do the same thing again, on purpose
cells.ask: Offer: begin one session as if you had never done this before — same drill, no history in your hands — and see what stays open, available, fresh.
cells.core:
You're lit and you're practicing, and the two haven't cancelled each other out. Something in you is still catching — not pointed at a goal yet, just alive — and instead of chasing it off somewhere new, you're bringing it to the same small work you did yesterday. The repetition hasn't dulled the spark; the spark hasn't scattered the repetition.

That's a rare steadiness, and it isn't finished. If you want more of it, here's where it goes next: let one session start from nothing. Same practice, but you arrive as a beginner to it — no score from last week, no idea what it should feel like. See how much of the work is still new when you let it be.
cells.sheetLine: You keep the spark and the practice in the same room.

cells.tense: Future — bracing at a beginning that hasn't happened yet.
cells.verb: igniting over and over without picking a direction
cells.place: in the quiet hour that was meant for doing the same thing again
cells.ask: Offer: look at what you have actually practiced, all of it, in plain light — not to judge it, just to see it whole — and notice how much is already there without you needing to prove it.
cells.core:
You keep lighting it. Every time you sit down to practice, some part of you starts over — a new approach, a new thing to try, a better version of what this could become — and the hour meant for repetition becomes an hour of beginnings. Somewhere ahead is the day you'll finally have started the right thing, and you're living toward that day so hard the practice itself never gets to be boring enough to work.

The spark isn't the problem. It just has nowhere to land while you keep striking it. What might help isn't more fire — it's a clear look. Set the pieces out and see what you've actually done: the hours, the small gains, the parts that are already yours. Nothing hidden, nothing to defend. When you can see it whole, you don't have to keep starting it. You get to show up open and ready instead of braced.
cells.sheetLine: You keep restarting the practice instead of practicing.

cells.tense: Past — still standing at a door that's already behind you.
cells.place: in the quiet hour where you still show up and do the same thing again
cells.ask: Offer: let yourself feel, fully, what this practice has connected you to — the people, the version of you it made — not to decide anything, just to know it; and let that knowing keep deepening rather than closing.
cells.core:
You're still doing the reps. You sit down, you go through it, you keep the light on — but nothing's catching. The practice remembers a beginning that isn't here anymore, and you're standing at the spot where it first lit, waiting for it to light the same way. It won't, and that's not a failure of the practice. It's just that the door is behind you now.

Trying harder at the empty hour won't fill it. What tends to bring the spark back is feeding what's just beneath it: the felt sense of why this ever mattered. Not the reasons — the feeling. Who you were connected to through it, what it let you be, what it still quietly means. Stay with that long enough and the hour stops being a ritual you're keeping for an old self. Something fresh starts moving through it again.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping the practice lit for a spark that already moved on.

cells.tense: Disowned present — pen down in a room you're already writing in.
cells.place: in the quiet hour you still call routine
cells.ask: Offer: say, once, to yourself or to someone, "something is starting in me" — before you know what it is or where it's going — and notice how much more available you are when you've admitted it.
cells.core:
Something has already caught. The practice has a different charge in it than it used to — you're reaching for things you didn't reach for, the reps are turning in a new direction, there's a pull you can feel when you sit down — and you describe all of it as just keeping up the routine. The beginning is happening. The one person who hasn't been told is you.

You don't have to know what it's for yet. That's the whole shape of this: a spark before direction, and it doesn't need a plan to be real. What it needs is to be claimed, at its simplest. Not "I'm going to become this" — just "something is starting." Say it once, plainly. The routine will still be there tomorrow. You'll just be arriving to it awake.
cells.sheetLine: Something's already starting in you. You're still calling it the routine.
